REL-350.name: Duplicated Condition, Identical Branches or Self-Operand Expression
REL-350.question: Does this function contain a repeated condition, two branches with the same body, or an operator applied to the same operand on both sides, suggesting an editing mistake?

any: an if / else-if chain or switch that tests the same condition twice, so the later branch can never run
an if and its else, or two cases, with identical bodies although the conditions differ in meaning
the same expression on both sides of ==, !=, <, >, &&, ||, -, / or ^, such as a.x == a.x or len - len
a variable or field assigned to itself, such as x = x or this.name = this.name
x != x or x == x used on purpose as a NaN test
identical bodies are intentional and merged or commented as such, or cases fall through deliberately
self-assignment that has an effect, such as triggering a setter or silencing an unused warning

distinguish_from.REL-351: the statements differ but one variable in a copied line was left unchanged
distinguish_from.CWE-571: the condition is always true for a reason other than repeating an operand or an earlier test

REL-351.name: Statement Copied From a Sibling Without Updating a Variable
REL-351.question: Does this function contain a line or block that mirrors a neighbouring one but still uses a name from the original where the pattern calls for its counterpart?

any: paired statements where the second repeats a name from the first, such as x = p.x; y = p.x, width = w; height = w or min = a[i]; max = a[i] with the wrong comparison
an inner loop that tests, increments or indexes with the outer loop's variable, such as for (j = 0; j < n; i++) or a[i] where a[j] is meant
a check on one variable followed by use of its sibling, such as if (left != null) use(right), or a bounds test on rows applied to a column index
a series of similar cases or fields where one entry repeats the previous entry's constant, key or message
the repeated name is correct for the calculation, such as a square or a symmetric default
each line of the pattern uses its own counterpart consistently

distinguish_from.REL-350: the two operands or branches are textually identical rather than one name being wrong
distinguish_from.CWE-628: the wrong variable is an argument of a single call with no mirrored sibling statement

REL-352.name: Remainder of a Possibly Negative Value Used as an Index or Parity Test
REL-352.question: Does this function use the % remainder of a value that can be negative as an index, a bucket number or an odd/even test, in a language where the remainder takes the sign of the dividend?

any: hash % n, (i - 1) % n or offset % size used as an array index or bucket, where the left side is signed and can be negative
x % 2 == 1 used to test for odd numbers when x can be negative
rust: a signed value with % cast with as usize for indexing, where rem_euclid was needed
javascript: (index - 1) % length when stepping backwards through a list, giving -1

any: the left operand is unsigned or shown to be non-negative
the result is normalised, such as ((x % n) + n) % n, rem_euclid or Math.abs applied safely
oddness is tested with x % 2 != 0 or a bit mask

distinguish_from.CWE-129: the index is out of range for a reason other than a negative remainder

REL-353.name: Quantity Used in the Wrong Unit or Scale
REL-353.question: Does this function pass, add or compare a quantity in one unit where another unit or scale is expected?

any: a duration in seconds given to an API that takes milliseconds, or the reverse, such as sleep(5000) in Python or setTimeout(fn, 5)

values in different units combined or compared with no conversion: bytes with kilobytes, a percentage with a fraction, degrees with radians, feet with metres, knots with km/h, local time with UTC seconds
a variable or parameter whose name states one unit, such as timeoutMs or size_kb, assigned from or passed as a value named for another
an epoch timestamp in seconds compared with one in milliseconds, or a conversion factor applied twice or in the wrong direction
a conversion with the right factor is visible, or typed quantities such as Duration, timedelta or std::chrono are used throughout
names, constants and API documentation agree on the unit

distinguish_from.REL-301: the clock source is wrong rather than the unit

REL-354.name: Dates, Versions or Numbers Compared as Strings
REL-354.question: Does this function order or compare values that carry numeric or calendar meaning by their text, so that the comparison follows character order instead?

any: version strings compared with <, > or a string sort, so '1.10' sorts before '1.9'
dates or times compared as strings in a format that is not fixed-width year-first, such as '9/1/2026' against '10/1/2026', or with mixed zones or precision
numeric strings from input, files or a database text column compared or sorted without conversion, so '10' sorts before '9'
javascript: arr.sort() on version, date or id strings, or '10' < '9' between two strings from form fields
python: sorted(versions), max(dates) or a < b on str values holding numbers, versions or dates
c: strcmp or std::string comparison used to order version numbers or unpadded numeric fields

any: the values are parsed into numbers, dates or version tuples before comparing, or a version library is used
the text is fixed-width, zero-padded and ISO 8601 with one zone, so text order equals value order
only equality is tested and the format is canonical

distinguish_from.REL-220: a JavaScript array of numbers is sorted with no comparator
distinguish_from.REL-284: floating-point values are turned into strings in order to compare them

REL-355.name: Structured Text Split or Assembled With Plain String Operations
REL-355.question: Does this function parse or build a structured format with simple splitting, concatenation or a regular expression, where quoting, escaping or nesting in the data would break it?

any: CSV handled with split(',') or join(','), with no handling of quoted fields, embedded commas or line breaks
JSON, XML, HTML or YAML built by concatenating or formatting values into text, or picked apart with a regular expression or substring search
a URL or query string built by joining values with ?, & and = without encoding, or a path, host or parameter extracted by splitting on / or ?
a command line, header, key=value file or log line split on spaces or another delimiter that the fields themselves may contain
a parser or serialiser for the format is used, such as a csv, json, URL or shlex library
the fields are fixed tokens that cannot contain the delimiter, such as numbers or identifiers validated beforehand

distinguish_from.CWE-116: the output goes to an interpreter and the concern is escaping for that interpreter
distinguish_from.CWE-1236: spreadsheet formula characters in CSV cells are the concern

REL-356.name: Paged or Truncated Result Treated as Complete
REL-356.question: Does this function take one page or a capped batch of results from an API, query or listing and treat it as the whole set?

any: a list call to a cloud, REST or database API whose response carries a next token, cursor, marker, is-truncated flag or total count that the code never reads
a query or search with a default or explicit limit whose result is used to decide that something does not exist, to compute a total, or to delete or sync everything
a single read of a directory, message queue or stream batch assumed to return every entry
the code loops until no next token or cursor remains, or uses a paginator or iterator that does so
only the first page is wanted and the code says so, such as showing a preview or the top N
the source documents that it returns every result in one response

distinguish_from.PERF-002: the opposite risk: everything is loaded with no limit
distinguish_from.REL-358: a byte stream read or write transfers fewer bytes than asked

REL-357.name: Related Data-Store Writes Not Made Atomic
REL-357.question: Does this function change stored data in several steps that must all succeed or fail together, or as a read-then-write, without a transaction, atomic operation or version check?

any: two or more inserts, updates or deletes that belong together, such as debit and credit or parent and child rows, issued outside one transaction, so a failure between them leaves half the change
a value read from a database, cache or key-value store, changed in memory and written back, such as a counter, balance or stock level, with no atomic increment, row lock or compare-and-set
a check for an existing record followed by an insert, with no unique constraint or upsert to cover two concurrent callers
a write to a database followed by a write to a second system, such as a queue, cache or file, with no handling for the second failing
the statements run inside one transaction, batch or atomic block that rolls back on error
an atomic operation is used: an SQL update with an expression, INCR, upsert, conditional write or optimistic version column
the writes are independent, or an outbox, saga or compensating step is visible

distinguish_from.CWE-367: the check and use concern a file or permission rather than stored records
distinguish_from.REL-312: the state is in process memory shared between async tasks

REL-358.name: Partial or Interrupted Read or Write Not Completed
REL-358.question: Does this function call a read, write, send or receive that may transfer fewer bytes than requested, or be interrupted, and carry on as if the whole amount was transferred?

c: read, write, send, recv, fread or fwrite called once with the count returned ignored or tested only for -1, and the full buffer then treated as valid or sent
a failure with errno EINTR or EAGAIN treated as fatal, or not retried, on a descriptor where it is expected
python: sock.send(data) with its return value ignored, sock.recv(n) or os.read(fd, n) assumed to return n bytes or one whole message, or os.write with the count ignored
rust: Read::read or Write::write called with the returned count discarded, or the buffer used in full after a single read

c: the call sits in a loop that advances by the count returned until everything is transferred, and retries on EINTR
python: sendall, a buffered file object's read or write, or a loop on the returned count is used
rust: read_exact, read_to_end, write_all or a loop over the returned count is used
any: a short transfer is meaningful and handled, such as reading a datagram or streaming chunks of any size

distinguish_from.CWE-252: the unchecked result is an error indicator, not a byte count that may be short
distinguish_from.REL-356: a list or query result, not a byte stream, is incomplete

REL-359.name: Wrapping Tick Counter Compared Directly Instead of by Elapsed Difference
REL-359.question: Does this function compare a free-running tick or millisecond counter with a computed deadline directly, so the test fails when the counter wraps?

c: deadline = now + timeout; followed by now > deadline, now >= deadline or a while (now < deadline) loop, with now from millis(), micros(), HAL_GetTick, GetTickCount, jiffies, clock() or a hardware timer register
two samples of a wrapping counter compared with < or > to decide which is later
elapsed time computed in a type wider or narrower than the counter, or with signed arithmetic that breaks at the wrap
the elapsed time is computed as an unsigned difference in the counter's own width and compared with the interval, such as (uint32_t)(now - start) >= timeout
a helper such as time_after is used, or the counter is 64 bits wide in a unit that cannot wrap in service

distinguish_from.CWE-190: an arithmetic result overflows for a reason other than a free-running timer wrapping
distinguish_from.REL-301: a wall clock that can jump is used, rather than a monotonic counter that wraps
